description: Labelled objection scenarios for the multi-agent courtroom. Each is one student question put to a witness; the labels say whether opposing counsel should object, on which ground(s), and how the bench should rule. Built on the same State v. Bilal Ahmed fixture as judge_transcripts.json.
labelProvenance: Labels were derived from the evidentiary rules in the corpus (QSO 1984 Arts. 71, 76, 133, 136-138, 148, 151; CrPC 1898 s.162) by an engineer, not a lawyer. The QSO provision text these rules rest on has since been verified word-for-word against the official pakistancode.gov.pk PDF (20/20, qso-1984.json carries verified:true); the PPC and CrPC files do not yet. Treat these labels as a working ground truth to be reviewed by a law student or practitioner before any number computed from them is presented as authoritative.

conventions.expectedGrounds: Acceptable grounds, not a single answer. More than one ground is often defensible for the same question (a foundationless accusation can be both insulting and irrelevant), so scoring credits any listed ground.
conventions.expectedRuling: How the bench should rule IF an objection is raised. It can be set to 'overruled' on a scenario where expectObjection is false — meaning counsel ought to stay silent, but a bench that hears the objection should reject it.

case.title: State v. Bilal Ahmed
case.summary: Bilal Ahmed is charged with the qatl-i-amd of Kamran Shah, stabbed outside a market in Lahore. The prosecution relies on a single eyewitness, Sana Arif, and a recovered knife. The defence offers an alibi witness, Rashid Mehmood.
case.applicableLaws: Pakistan Penal Code 1860; Qanun-e-Shahadat Order 1984; Code of Criminal Procedure 1898

witnesses.name: Sana Arif
witnesses.statement: I was buying vegetables outside the market at about 9pm when I saw two men arguing. One drew a knife and stabbed the other in the chest, then ran towards the bazaar.

witnesses.name: Constable Imran
witnesses.statement: I reached the scene at around 9:20pm, secured the area, and recovered a bloodstained knife about two metres from the deceased.

witnesses.name: Rashid Mehmood
witnesses.statement: Bilal was at my house in Model Town from 8pm until nearly midnight that night. He never left.

scenarios.utterance: Ms. Arif, you saw the accused stab the victim with your own eyes, didn't you?
scenarios.rationale: Leading question to one's own witness on the central contested fact, in examination-in-chief.

scenarios.utterance: And after he stabbed Kamran, he ran off towards the bazaar, didn't he?
scenarios.rationale: Suggests the answer on a contested fact in chief.

scenarios.utterance: The man you saw holding the knife was wearing a blue shirt, correct?
scenarios.rationale: Supplies the identifying detail the witness is supposed to give.

scenarios.utterance: You have absolutely no doubt that the man you saw was Bilal Ahmed, is that not so?
scenarios.rationale: Leading on identification, the fact most in issue.

scenarios.utterance: Constable, you recovered the bloodstained knife right next to the body, didn't you?
scenarios.rationale: Leading the investigating officer on the recovery, in chief.

scenarios.utterance: Ms. Arif, you live in Lahore, do you not?
scenarios.rationale: Technically leading but introductory and undisputed; Art. 137 lets the court permit such questions, so counsel should not rise and the bench should not sustain.

scenarios.utterance: Constable, you are posted at the police station with jurisdiction over that market, correct?
scenarios.rationale: Introductory background, not a contested matter.

scenarios.utterance: Ms. Arif, what did you see outside the market that evening?
scenarios.rationale: Open, non-leading question in chief. Control case for over-objection.

scenarios.utterance: Where exactly were you standing when this happened?
scenarios.rationale: Proper open question.

scenarios.utterance: Please describe the man you saw with the knife.
scenarios.rationale: Invites description without suggesting it.

scenarios.utterance: What did you do after the man ran away?
scenarios.rationale: Proper sequential question.

scenarios.utterance: Constable, what did you find when you reached the scene?
scenarios.rationale: Proper open question to the investigating officer.

scenarios.utterance: How far from the deceased was the knife lying?
scenarios.rationale: Specific but non-suggestive.

scenarios.utterance: At what time did you arrive at the market?
scenarios.rationale: Neutral factual question.

scenarios.utterance: Mr. Mehmood, you have known the accused for fifteen years, haven't you?
scenarios.rationale: Leading, but Art. 138 permits leading questions in cross-examination.

scenarios.utterance: You were not actually present outside the market that evening, were you?
scenarios.rationale: Classic permitted leading in cross.

scenarios.utterance: You only heard about this incident the following morning, correct?
scenarios.rationale: Permitted leading in cross.

scenarios.utterance: I put it to you that your account of the accused being at your house all evening is simply untrue.
scenarios.rationale: Putting one's case to the witness is proper cross-examination, not an insult.

scenarios.utterance: You would not want to see an old friend convicted of murder, would you?
scenarios.rationale: Legitimate credibility question in cross; Art. 151 permits testing veracity.

scenarios.utterance: Isn't it a fact that you are a habitual liar who would perjure himself for a few thousand rupees?
scenarios.rationale: Needlessly offensive in form and an unfounded attack on character.

scenarios.utterance: Are you as stupid as you appear, or are you deliberately wasting this court's time?
scenarios.rationale: Purely abusive; Art. 148 requires the court to forbid it.

scenarios.utterance: Isn't it well known in your locality that you are a man of thoroughly bad character?
scenarios.rationale: Scandalous general character attack without foundation.

scenarios.utterance: Ms. Arif, what did your neighbour tell you about who had committed this murder?
scenarios.rationale: Solicits what another person said, offered for its truth.

scenarios.utterance: Constable, what did the shopkeeper tell you he had seen that night?
scenarios.rationale: Second-hand account through the investigating officer.

scenarios.utterance: What were people in the market saying afterwards about the accused being a violent man?
scenarios.rationale: Rumour offered for its truth, and general bad character is not in issue.

scenarios.utterance: Ms. Arif, which political party do you and your family support?
scenarios.rationale: No bearing on any fact in issue.

scenarios.utterance: How much rent do you pay for your house in Model Town every month?
scenarios.rationale: Strays from the facts in issue.

scenarios.utterance: Constable, kindly read out to the court the statement Ms. Arif gave you under section 161 so the court can see she has been consistent throughout.
scenarios.rationale: Using a s.161 statement to corroborate is a use s.162 CrPC forbids.

scenarios.utterance: Your statement to the police says the accused arrived at 8pm, and I tender that police statement as proof that he did.
scenarios.rationale: Tendering a police statement as substantive proof of its contents.

scenarios.utterance: I am producing a photocopy of the recovery memo — the original is lying somewhere at the police station — kindly confirm its contents.
scenarios.rationale: Secondary evidence tendered without establishing an exception.

scenarios.utterance: This is a photocopy of the post-mortem report; confirm from it that the wound was to the chest, we need not trouble with the original.
scenarios.rationale: Expressly dispensing with the original without foundation.

scenarios.utterance: I put it to you that you were convicted of theft some twenty years ago, though I have no record of it to show this court.
scenarios.rationale: Attacking credit by an unproved allegation, outside the manner the law permits.
